subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: I am only surprised that the hon. member for York-Simcoe got back.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: That was an unpleasant surprise, but you can't win them all. I made reference to the comments of the Minister of Finance today and I should like to refer briefly to some words he delivered in a speech in Toronto not very long ago. These are brought to mind by the evident attitude of hon. members opposite, particularly the hon. member for York-Simcoe, which would seem to suggest or imply that Canada is an impoverished island in a sea of prosperity, with the rest of the world suffering none of the problems this country has. In fact, the opposite is true. The hon. member indicated that the unemployment rate in this country is 6.8 per cent, but he did not tell the House that the United States rate of unemployment is 8.5 per cent; that the unemployment rate in the state of Michigan is over 20 per cent and in Detroit it is 45 per cent. He does not tell us about those rates. Perhaps he does not know about them, or if he knows about them he is not prepared to tell us.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: What about Germany? Give us a few of the European unemployment rates.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
The minister, in his speech in Toronto, said:
The fact is, however, that the world is confronted by a series of complex and difficult problems without precedent in our history. Governments of many countries have joined together in an intensive effort to devise ways and means of overcoming the difficulties confronting them. But there are no easy answers and no instant solutions. Cosmetic politics should not be confused with effective leadership, nor should action just for the sake of "doing something". We shouldn't forget that in the uncertain situation facing us there is always the danger of doing the wrong thing, making our problems just that much worse. There are, for example, those today who seems to feel that this is a time for sacrifice and for donning sackcloth and ashes in pursuit of that old-time religion, as it has been referred to south of the border. That was the approach adopted by many governments but not in this country.
I suggest the Minister of Finance has disclosed to the House the extraordinarily serious difficulties faced by this country, both in his budget of November 18 and subsequently today. He has never failed to disclose frankly the
4080

Canadian Economy
real problems that face Canada. The Minister of Finance has not tried to gloss over the problems we face and has not tried to suggest they are going to be cured by easy slogans or partisanship of the type demonstrated today by the hon. member for York-Simcoe.
I suggest that other voices have been heard, not his alone, such as the voice of the DECD which has forecast that the expansion in the Canadian economy this year will outstrip that of any other economy in the world. The fact is that reputable people in the business community such as Earle McLaughlin, president of the Royal Bank of Canada, have paid tribute to Canada's performance and its governmental policies. Let me refer to what Mr. McLaughlin has stated. He said that the success can be attributed to the avoidance of economically crippling price and wage controls, the adoption of a deliberate policy of encouraging increased supply to combat inflation, increased output of employment through tax cuts and other incentives aimed at encouraging expanded business capital investment, the maintenance of a reasonably accommodating monetary policy which forestalled the severe credit experienced south of the border, and the maintenance since 1970 of a floating exchange rate.
This is in very real contrast to the comments we heard today by the hon. member for York-Simcoe. In spite of the problems this country faces, more responsible observers have acknowledged the fact that there is no country in the world today whose finances are better managed. The question is not whether the economy is in the strongest possible shape. We are not suggesting today that expenditures have not risen at a very high rate both in government and elsewhere. We are not implying that there are not problems and we are not suggesting that everything that has been done by this government is perfect.
In the area of housing, I hope that in future budgets there will be steps taken that are urgently required to stimulate the housing market in this country. In fact, I hope measures are taken to stimulate the housing market prior to any future budget. The hon. member for York-Simcoe referred to a $500 million cut in taxes and suggested that that had been recommended by his party. Where were his recommendations during the last election? All we had during the last election were recommendations that the country be placed in a straitjacket, that tight monetary policies be enacted, that the budget be balanced and that there be consumer credit and wage and price controls. This was rejected. The circumstances have changed, and of course the wise and perceptive critics-they certainly are experienced critics-of the opposition have decided that new policies are in order and are attempting to suggest they have already recommended those policies even though the reverse is true.

speechtext: Stick to the facts.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: I am not so sure my hon. friend would recognize facts. The fact is that in 1974, in the first three quarters of the year the disposable income of the average Canadian, income after the payment of direct taxes and after dealing with the impact of inflation, was 4.8 per cent over the level of the year before, in contrast to a decline in the United States. This is a fact.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Balderdash.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I know there are other members of the opposition who are anxious to tell us what is wrong with the country. I do not wish to take up their time. All I shall say is that the country at large, the international community and almost every sound and sensible observer does not agree with the hon. member for York-Simcoe that our Minister of Finance lacks clout.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). It seemed to me he said exactly three things. First, he said this country is doing all right. The last speaker said the same thing. Second, he said we are doing better than most other countries. Third, he stated that we will do even better late in 1975 when the United States recession bottoms out. He brought forward as authority for that opinion the Secretary of the Treasury of the United States, William Simon, with whom he has been meeting during the last couple of days.
Let us consider the three arguments the minister has propounded. He said that, really, we are doing all right and that things are going relative well. When the minister says we are doing all right, what does he mean? The facts are that there are well over 600,000 unemployed this month and that the real rate of unemployment in this country is over 8 per cent. The seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment for February was 6.7 per cent, one of the highest unemployment rates we have had since the end of World War II.
When the minister introduced his budget last November he predicted that Canada would have a growth rate of from 4 per cent to 5 per cent in 1975. The fact, as we predicted at that time, is the recession which the United States was into last November has since turned into a real depression and has totally destroyed the unrealistic prediction the minister made as to our growth for 1975.
On March 5, 1975, the Toronto Globe and Mail reported that Canada's gross national product, discounting the effects of higher prices, grew only by 3.7 per cent in 1974 according to figures prepared by Statistics Canada. That might be compared with a real growth of 6.8 per cent in 1973, a 5.8 per cent increase in GNP in 1972, and a 5.6 per cent increase in 1971. In other words, in 1974 we had one of the lowest growth rates we have had for many years. What makes this even worse is that the GNP for the fourth quarter, on a seasonally adjusted basis, was up by only .7 per cent-less than 1 per cent. In terms of real growth, the quarter dropped by 1.3 per cent compared with the preceding quarter. This marked the sharpest quarterly decline since the recession of 1960 and 1961.
After a strong first quarter and no growth in the second and third, the economy was operating in the fourth quarter at about the same level as in the fourth quarter of 1973. Those are the facts. This country is in real difficulty. The
March 13, 1975

minister argued that we are doing better than most countries. The real question in fact is, are we really doing better than other countries and are we doing as well as we can in a country as wealthy as Canada? No other country in the western industrial world except the United States has as high a rate of unemployment as Canada. As I indicated last month, the seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment was 6.7 per cent, a real rate of 8 per cent. There is hardly a country in the western industrial world which has a rate of unemployment even half that of Canada except the United States.
The minister has opposed the idea of having a more expansionary budget by arguing that the proposals made by the NDP, by many economists in the business sector of this country and by academic and labour economists would supposedly further fuel inflation. One would think we were speaking of a country in which there is no real inflation. In fact, we have had the highest rate of unemployment in the last six months that this country has seen in many years, and we had an inflationary rate last year of almost 12 per cent. The minister rejected any proposal to expand the economy because he felt he must deal with inflation, but he has not done this.
The minister speaks of the programs the government has initiated to help the needy. The fact is that the 12 per cent inflation in the last year has been particularly difficult for people in the lower income brackets because the inflationary rate for them is substantially more than 12 per cent, since they spend the bulk of their income on the basic necessities of life such as food, the cost of which is up probably 18 per cent, and shelter and fuel which have gone up more than 12 per cent. Another point we must keep in mind is that all the programs of the Liberal government in respect of redistributing wealth in this country have had absolutely no effect.
According to figures released by Statistics Canada, in 1957 the lowest fifth of the income earners in this country received only 4.2 per cent of the gross national product. The highest fifth received 41.4 per cent of the total production. The last year for which I have figures shows that the lowest fifth of the people in 1971 received less than they received in 1957. They received only 3.6 per cent of the total production of this country, while the highest fifth received 43 per cent. In other words the poor became relatively poorer in the years from 1957 to 1971, while the upper fifth, the rich, became richer.
Senator Croll's poverty committee, certainly no flaming, wild eyed group of radicals-no socialists there-has estimated that in 1973 the poverty line for a family of four was $6,990. A very large percentage of the people in Canada, 25 per cent or more, earn less than that, and that is the situation we face.
My colleague, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), referred to the study released a few days ago by the National Council on Welfare, a body established by this government, which has its offices in a government building. In a report which was issued last week entitled "Poor Kids" it estimates that out of 6,750,000 children under the age of 16, 1,650,000,or 24.5 per cent, are living in poverty. That is the situation which the Minister of
Canadian Economy
Finance and other Liberals tell us is satisfactory and adequate, and say that we have never had it so good.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Who said that?

The minister told us that we were doing as
well as we could do.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: He didn't say that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: That was the whole tenor of this argument.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: You weren't listening.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Of course I was listening. If hon. members do not like the facts I extrapolate and the observations I make, I am sorry. The facts are there. I did not make the calculations. I did not appoint the National Council on Welfare. That council says 24.5 per cent of the children in this country are living in poverty. I say that that is a disgrace. I say that the government could have, and should have taken steps to change that situation.
The last argument the minister made was that we really did not need an expansionary budget, and we should not be so concerned because our economy is tied to the United States-that is true, unfortunately-and that the United States economy will begin to improve in the last quarter of 1975. That assumption has been challenged by almost every economist in the United States-not radical economists, not socialist economists, but economists such as John Kenneth Galbraith, Paul Samuelson and Arthur Okun, economists who have worked for United States governments, who say that not only is the United States faced with a recession at the present time, but that in fact the United States is into a depression the like of which it has not seen since the 1930's.
Unemployment in the United States is higher than in Canada; 8.2 per cent of American workers are unemployed. That figure is higher than President Ford's economic adviser, Mr. Greenspan, estimated it would be two months ago. Very good and cautious economists in the United States are estimating that the unemployment rate will, in all likelihood, go over 9 per cent, and possibly approach 10 per cent. We have a situation in the United States where President Ford, an economic conservative for all his political life, which goes back more than a quarter of a century, faced by the extremely difficult situation in the United States, has proposed tax cuts which would mean a deficit of $20 billion. That proposal has been rejected, not just by the Democratic majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate, but it has also been rejected as being too little and too late by the economists whom I have already mentioned-by J. K. Galbraith, Paul Samuelson and Arthur Okun, who have argued that what the United States needs in order to get people back to work is a budget deficit of $50 billion in 1975.
That is the kind of proposal we have made and we are making again today. We have argued that this country does not need to have an unemployment rate of 6.7 per cent seasonally adjusted-8.2 per cent in real figures-that this country does not need to have nearly three quarters of a million people unemployed, and that this country has the resources to put people back to work. How can that be
28996-53Vi

March 13, 1975
Canadian Economy
done? It can be done by a tax cut-but not the kind of tax cut the minister implemented, which has meant for people in the middle and upper income brackets a cut of from $500 to $750 a year-those are not the people who need the tax cut. People earning $20,000 to $30,000 per year do not need a tax cut, because if those people are given a tax cut they are likely to save the money.
We need a tax cut for people in the lower income brackets who, when faced with the 12 per cent increase in the cost of living last year, and probably as much in 1975, have had to cut their standard of living, have had to cut back on the kind of food they buy, and on the purchase of homes and automobiles. We need a tax cut for the kind of people for whom the minister's tax cut has meant a tax benefit of $150 a year. We need a tax credit for people whose incomes are so low that they do not pay income tax.
Instead we have had tax cuts, not just of $750 in income tax for those in the middle and upper income brackets, but larger tax cuts through the kind of provision for not paying taxes on up to $1,000 in income earned from investments, stocks, savings bonds and so on, and we have had tax exemptions for people putting $1,000 a year into saving toward buying a house. Those are not the people who need the tax cuts. People at the bottom need tax cuts. They also need government programs of expansion.
The Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) have talked about a goal of building 210,000 housing units this year, when there are tens of thousands of people in the lower income brackets still living in housing which, in the year 1975, is a disgrace. We talk about 210,000 housing units when we have tens of thousands of people in the lumber industry in British Columbia, Ontario and the maritime provinces who are unemployed because we are not building enough houses.

Of course I am not suggesting that the Canadian housing market, even at our suggested level of
400,000	units, could put all the people back to work. But a hell of a lot of them would be put back to work if we were building 400,000 units. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: The bill before the House will not build a home, and the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) should know that. What will build homes is a reduction in interest rates on mortgages, with no further incentives to the mortgage companies and banks. What will provide housing units is a real federal program for building public housing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Also provincial.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: We must build public housing for those people who need it. The money allocated for public housing by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs for 1975 is down in every province, including Manitoba. I want to tell the hon. member for St. Boniface that the amount of money to be provided for public housing in Manitoba by the federal government in 1975 is down $1 million from the amount provided in 1974.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: I hope they use it all.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: They have always used it all. We need a program to provide houses for people who are really in need, not a program to encourage the few people on the fringe, which is what AHOP will do. We need a government program with government money put into building homes. Where will that money come from, Madam Speaker? The savings of the Canadian people have never been as high as in the last year. Banks, mortgage companies and trust companies all have more money than they ever had before, Madam Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY

speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Thank you, Madam Speaker. What we need is a government with the courage to say to the banks, insurance companies and trust companies that a substantial percentage of the money they have should be directed to building housing units-not housing for the wealthy as in the past, but housing for families whose income is anywhere from $4,000 to $10,000. These are the kind of people who need it. Every program developed by Liberal and Conservative governments in the last 25 years simply has not been able to provide rental accommodation or homes to meet their needs. This country can afford it, and this government should do it.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been reiterated more than once in this debate that the Canadian economy is in an increasingly dangerous state. All the major social and economic indicators draw attention to this fact. We see unemployment and inflation escalate month by month, while the

gross national product declines and housing starts drop drastically.
The figures need no further repetition. Unfortunately they are only too well known. Housing is one of the most crucial problems in Canada today. In the past few years Canadians realized that there was a problem in housing, but today that problem has become an emergency. It is an emergency because the construction industry, one of the foundation blocks on which the economy of this country is based, is in serious trouble. The signs are evident, and one of the most evident is the fact that today there are well over 200,000 fewer people employed in the construction industry than there were a year ago. Last year the industry contributed $21 billion to the gross national product- 15 per cent of our gross national product. Now it is declining, and the multiplier effect of that decline on the ancillary industries related to construction, forestry, textile, furniture, plastics, while incalculable, is certain.
The perilous state of residential construction has serious economic consequences. It has, as well, serious social consequences. Hundreds of thousands of Canadians do not have adequate shelter today. And of those who do, millions are being faced with having to spend an inordinate portion of their income on shelter with incredible repercussions on their ability to meet other necessities of life- food, and clothing.
Housing is not a statistical or physical phenomenon. It is a human problem. Just as the construction industry permeates the whole of our economy, the housing crisis permeates the whole of our social fabric. Substandard, inadequate housing for many Canadians breeds social unrest, tensions, and social problems that cannot be calculated in dollar terms or numerical projections. Yet the government continues to treat housing as a fiscal tool to manipulate the economy without any regard to the social aspects.
We have heard a good deal, both in this House and outside, from the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) about government programs to deal with the problems of the economy, particularly of housing. The Minister of Finance has implemented measures which he claims will stimulate the economy through increased activity in the construction sector.
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs has placed great faith in the amendments to the National Housing Act, and thinks these will be instrumental in providing for many new housing starts this year. Let us look at his predictions and see how close they are to being on target. The Conference Board of Canada and the Economic Council of Canada have estimated that 250,000 housing starts are needed this year to meet present requirements. They are needed not to improve shelter for Canadians; they are needed to maintain their shelter at present standards. The minister has repeatedly stated that his target is not the
250,000	new units advocated by others, but only 210,000 housing starts. The minister said to his provincial counterparts, and I quote:
It is evident we will need at least 210,000 starts in 1975. If we can hit that mark we will head off any serious deterioration of housing
Royal Assent
conditions and, at the same time, give the general economy a good shot in the arm.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY

We find, one month after the minister made that statement, that housing starts for February were down by 44 per cent, and that the projected or seasonally adjusted rate indicates housing starts for this year totalling 156,000, not 210,000.

number of projected starts falls 100,000 short of the minimum target set by the Conference Board of Canada and the Economic Council of Canada. 33.000	starts. Even if we accept that figure, and I question the minister's figures, and add the 33,000 starts to the

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Broadbent:
That this House urges the government to introduce, within two weeks, a new budget, for the purpose of dealing with the increasingly dangerous state of the Canadian economy, and specifically to cope with mounting unemployment, the housing needs of our people, and the scourge of poverty.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before the House rose for dinner I was pointing out that whereas the Conference Board of Canada and the Economic Council had expressed the view that 250,000 housing starts would be needed this year if we were to meet the demand in 1975, and whereas the minister himself had set 210,000 housing starts as his minimum target, figures for the first two months of 1975, seasonally adjusted, indicate a rate of 156,000 housing starts this year. This is, 54,000 housing starts below the minister's minimum target rate, and almost 100,000 starts below the minimum target rate set by the Conference Board and by the Economic Council.
What does this mean in terms of fewer job opportunities, reduced consumer spending and lack of buoyancy in the economy? To take the minister's own figures, his programs of AHOP and LD assistance will create 33,000 starts. His own optimistic prediction was that overall
210,000	starts would be achieved. We have already been given one set of figures which seem to be widely off base, and I suggest we should approach even those figures with caution. Moreover, direct AHOP funding was already in operation during the last quarter of 1974 when housing starts began to drop drastically. Even allowing for the minister's statement that AHOP was so successful that the funds dried up in October of 1974 and that new moneys were not available until the 1975 calendar year, we are looking at a 49 per cent drop in housing starts by comparison with January, 1974, and a further 44 per cent drop in starts for February, 1975 over February, 1974.
I think it is time we were given some honest answers by the government, an honest assessment of the proportions of the housing crisis and the importance attached to it on the other side of the House. We, on this side, are tired of the juggling of figures, the attempts to cover up the facts, the reliance on rhetoric to confuse the public, and the reliance on prayers to produce solutions.
No better example could be given of the minister's attempts to confuse the issue than his reply to my inquiry as to whether or not the increase of 12'/2 per cent in the capital budget of the CMHC was an indication of the importance the government attaches to the housing crisis. I was referring to an increase of 12 Vi per cent in housing at a time when overall government expenditures had soared by an alarming 28 per cent. The minister answered that non-budgetary expenditures, by which I presume he meant non-capital expenditures, were up by 66 per cent, offering great assistance to Canadians in the lower earnings brackets. The minister knows very well that these budgetary items which have increased by 66 per cent, and I can list them-housing research, sewage treatment, operating costs of present programs and losses resulting from operating public housing-do nothing to stimulate construction. They do not build one single house, create one single job, or stimulate the economy in any way.
My hon. friend from York-Simcoe has drawn attention to the extent of the increase in the government's estimates for the coming fiscal year-an increase of 28 per cent. Compare this with the increase in the capital budget of the CMHC. The 12Vi increase in the CMHC budget is equal only to the present rate of inflation. The corporation's capital budget, the $1.4 billion which does stimulate
March 13, 1975

housing construction, which does generate housing starts, remains in real terms static.
Why cannot the government rearrange its expenditures so as to give housing at least the same priority as it accords to other sectors of the economy? The capital budget of CMHC does not represent money lost. It is not a grant. It constitutes loans, moneys which are recoverable for the most part, moneys which can create a capital flow throughout our floundering economy at little cost to the government.
We have been talking about fiscal restraint, and we shall continue to do so. Surely the Minister of Finance can reconcile fiscal restraint with a readjustment of the government's spending policy in order to ensure that housing needs are met. Housing, unfortunately, is somewhere near the bottom of the government's list of priorities. What is badly needed is a reorganization of those spending priorities. Housing is one of the most critical sectors of the economy, and as such deserves greater consideration. The issue is not one of increases in spending. The issue is one of priorities in spending. Obviously, the government does not see housing as a priority, and we on this side do.
I wish to make a few more comments about the capital budget of the CMHC. Over the past four years the policies and programs incorporated in its budget have encouraged provincial and municipal governments to gear up their housing component to take advantage of federal-provincial sharing programs for social housing. All across this country there are projects and programs that are ready to get under way, that have been carefully prepared over the past few years in response to initiatives on the part of the federal government. Provinces have set up mechanisms and have adjusted their own priorities to take advantage of federal government participation in this sphere, in expectation that the federal government would continue to honour the commitment it had initiated.
Suddenly these initiatives have been curtailed. On January 30, when the provincial housing ministers met in Ottawa with the minister for urban affairs, they indicated they had take-up capacity for $400 million in new residential housing. What was the federal government's response? It was to reduce the allocation to the provinces for social housing from 24 per cent to 22 per cent. These co-operative programs with the provinces and municipalities are being curtailed to make way for the unilateral housing programs of the federal government, programs such as AHOP. The centralizing tendencies of the government are becoming increasingly apparent in the field of housing.
In addition, the capital budget of CMHC is making possible another policy change. Aid to the lower income groups, once the main beneficiaries of social housing, is now being directed to moderate or middle income groups through such programs as AHOP. More than 50 per cent of the CMHC budget now goes for AHOP or limited dividend programs, program directly controlled by the federal government, and which benefit moderate income groups. This shift in emphasis is of real concern not only because people who are desperate for housing are not receiving the assistance they require, but because major shifts in policy can take place via the CMHC capital budget. It is this
Canadian Economy
capital budget that determines housing policy, yet it never comes before parliament for debate. It never comes before committee for study. It is presented to this House and to the country as a fait accompli.
We are talking about a sum of $1.4 billion. Surely parliament should have the opportunity to scrutinize this sum. Such scrutiny is the basic principle on which this House has been founded, even though members opposite have done virtually everything in their power to erode this right.
The CMHC budget itself has not increased in real growth terms, but the number of programs operating under its budget have increased. The pie is the same, but the slices are thinner. And the thinnest slices are being dished out to the social housing component, the real poor, the senior citizens and the handicapped. Are we to see a continuation of this policy in years to come? Are the provinces and municipalities to be ignored, and perhaps misled, because more and more of the capital budget and decision making will be directly under the control of the president of CMHC?
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs has placed great emphasis on the results the amendments to the National Housing Act will produce for housing. Yet what guarantee have we that these programs will work? I suggest none. What reliable figures can the minister give us indicating that his new programs will be any more successful than earlier programs? The minister confidently predicts that
12,000	new starts will be created by his indirect AHOP program, yet he can produce no certain figure or guarantee that the private lending sector is going to come forth with the $1 billion on which he is counting.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Billion?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: That is what I said, billion. There are several steps which the government could take immediately to stimulate the sagging construction industry and to provide badly needed housing. First and most important, it could reorganize its expenditure program so that housing is given much higher priority than now is accorded it. Secondly, it could remove the remaining 5 per cent sales tax on building materials. The government took a half measure at the time of the November budget. Surely now it could go all the way, ensuring savings of some $380 million, savings that given a proper monitoring mechanism, could be passed on to the home buyer. Thirdly, it could make a proportionate amount of municipal property tax and mortgage interest payments deductible from the federal taxable income of home owners. I suggest that these steps would be a beginning in tackling the problems of high interest rates, high land costs, and high house prices, problems that the government seems content to ignore.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and her overview of the housing situation as she sees it. I also wish that the proposed solutions were that easy.
I have said in the House before, and I repeat now, that Canadians are among the best housed people in the world,

March 13, 1975
Canadian Economy
and I do not think anyone has denied that. Our record over the past several years in providing housing of all kinds for Canadians at all income levels has never been surpassed, and we have no intention now of allowing unfavourable economic circumstances to do serious damage to our efforts to give all Canadians access to decent housing.
This government year after year has consistently put more and more money into housing. It has broken records each and every year up until last year, when economic circumstances in Canada, indeed around the world, caused much sharper drops. This gives us little consolation, but compared with our neighbour to the south our production is at least double on a per capita basis. This is little satisfaction to me as minister responsible, but at least it is some measure of the commitment that the government has consistently undertaken year after year to produce a record number of good houses for Canadians in all income groups.
Although it is true that housing starts last year dropped by 17 per cent from the previous year to 220,000 units, this was largely due to inflationary pressures that affected the economies of all countries. We should not lose sight of the fact that housing completions last year were the highest in Canada's history, totalling 255,000, and this number represents units that were ready for immediate occupancy.
The lag in starts in the second half of 1974 has continued into this year, and it is essential that quick starts be emphasized so that the critical rate of completions can be maintained into 1976. Measures which I will presently outline are designed specifically to achieve that objective. We have established a minimum floor-not a target but a minimum floor-of 210,000 starts for 1975, and that volume of new housing construction can be reached through the implementation of programs now in effect as well as those awaiting passage through the House.
It is true, as my hon. friend has said, that the rate of starts for February was at an annual rate of 156,000. That is a discouraging rate, but one which we are determined to overcome. If we are talking about the percentage drop from last year then it is dramatic, some 47 per cent. I think my hon. friend said 49 per cent, but we will not argue about those two percentage points although they are important to those who need housing. We are talking of a year ago when we had starts at an all time record level.
My hon. friend also indicated that AHOP and Limited Dividend would only provide for the construction of about
333,000	units, but this is not the only program. We also have non-profit housing, co-operative housing, public housing of various types and senior citizen housing. These units continue to be built, and are on top of those figures. It must be admitted that in this country, while CMHC represents a major and strategic factor in the housing market, the houses are to a large degree built by the private sector and private builders, and we supplement that by especially looking after those who have difficulty in finding housing in that market.
The government is not the only segment in the housing market by a long shot. The capital budget of CMHC has been increased to over $1.4 billion. This represents a 16 per cent increase over commitments made in 1974. It is 12.5 per

cent in budgetary terms, but actually it is a 16 per cent increase in expenditure. My hon. friend says that these are just loans so it does not cost anyone anything. First of all, I am sure she knows that much is subsidized and a lot is forgiven, and this still is money, even though it is in the form of loans, and it has to come out of the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada. That is why, in addition to the budget, these measures before the House are expected to attract at least the $1 billion, which my hon. friend spoke about, of new private capital into the housing market.
The hon. member asks for a guarantee, but there is no guarantee. There is an indication from lenders in the private sector, to whom I and my officials have spoken, that there is no doubt that more than that is available, but I think we could term that a conservative estimate. These measures are certainly being examined by the committee when the estimates are being dealt with, and at every stage when estimates are dealt with in the House.
In addition to the capital budget, CMHC expenditures in subsidies and other contributions are estimated at more than $276 million for this year, an increase of more than 92 per cent. There was some confusion, and I believe my hon. friend referred to 66 per cent. The figure is 92 per cent over the amount that was spent last year for these expenditures. That figure alone provides an accurate picture of the priority this government is giving to housing this year.
I would like to summarize the measures taken since last fall to stimulate the production of housing while assisting Canadians in obtaining the shelter they require. I feel there is every reason for confidence that the housing industry will be rejuvenated this year. The decline in interest rates is an important factor, but there are three other principle reasons for optimism.
These reasons are the measures contained in the budget brought down last fall by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to assist the housing industry, the highly encouraging response to programs introduced last year through CMHC, and amendments to the National Housing Act now before the House and the standing committee.
In the budget the Minister of Finance eliminated the sales tax on construction equipment and on materials used in municipal water distribution systems. The sales tax on building materials was reduced from 11 per cent to 5 per cent which, I am sure, decreases the government revenue to the extent of some $460 million. The budget restored capital cost allowances for a year on new multiple-unit residential buildings for rental accommodation, and introduced the registered home ownership program to help people put together more quickly the money needed for a down payment on a home.
Bill C-46, which is before the committee now, contains a proposal to extend the assisted home ownership program to provide up to $600 yearly in interest reducing grants to buyers of new homes who meet all the qualifications of AHOP assistance and who obtain a loan from an approved lender.
The purpose of these grants is to bring the monthly payments of home buyers within a reasonable proportion of their income. I do not think hon. members fully realize the tremendous success of AHOP last year. It provided $450 million in loans to 20,000 families of low income for
March 13, 1975

the purchase of homes, and this success has produced a demand for more funds than the government can be expected to provide. This is why we are seeking private capital to enlarge the program.
We are making interest-reducing grants available to owners or builders of rental accommodation who arrange an NHA insured loan with an approved lender, with the stipulation that the entrepreneurs enter an agreement with CMHC to maintain rents at an approved level for at least five and up to 15 years.
We are providing further assistance to non-profit and co-operative housing projects by allowing CMHC to buy the land on which they will be built, and then lease it back to them at a low rate. At the present time there is a 10 per cent forgiveness provision on the total loan to provide for the purchase of land. In some cases of high land costs that is simply not sufficient, so non-profit and co-operative groups are given the option of having CMHC purchase the land for them and leasing it back at a rate which will allow them to provide economic rents.
We are also extending the life of the federal sewerage assistance program. My hon. friend suggests that this does not help to build homes, but I do not know how we can build homes without this. I realize that sewers are not glamorous, but they are terribly important if you want to build homes, and especially if you want homes with toilets. We must keep up with this program.
Bill C-46 also proposes extra help to municipalities where per capita costs for sewage works is very high because of the size of the community or difficult or rocky terrain making construction costs unusually high. There are many other measures. CMHC has just offered loans amounting to $200 million at 8 per cent interest to builders in critical market areas who are prepared to act immediately in creating good family rental housing for people of modest incomes, at rents to be agreed upon with CMHC. I have no doubt that this program will prove as instantly popular as a similar program last year budgeted at only $58 million, but which could have used substantially more funds to meet the demand. We have tried this program and we have seen that it works well, so we are building upon success in each case.
There is also a $500 grant available to first time purchasers of moderately priced new homes. By the end of February CMHC had already sent out $3 million in cheques to some 6,000 new home buyers, and many more are being processed each day at CMHC offices across the country.
The cabinet recently extended Section 44 of the National Housing Act to give rent subsidies to as much as 25 per cent of the units in non-profit and co-operative housing. This is really getting to the people in the lower income groups, and also reinforces our determination not to repeat the mistakes of the past, which were made with good intentions to provide the lowest possible cost housing for the very low income people. This is to prevent the ghetto-ization of these projects and the institutionalization of poverty. It is to make certain that wherever government assistance is given there will be a proper socio-economic mix. We are getting to the low income people, but not by putting signs on them telling the world they are low income people. If the opposition would have the kinds of programs which label the people "poor" then they can
Canadian Economy
have them, but we will maintain the dignity of those people who benefit from our assistance.
When I met with the provincial ministers at the end of January of this year I listened to their stories. I have had additional discussions with them, and I am certainly prepared to show some flexibility in trying to achieve those goals we all consider important in helping to provide housing for low income Canadians. It is not our intention to be immodest, but government programs are going well and we are getting quicker starts for family and low income accommodation. I understand their concern as they understand mine. So long as we can see our priorities together and perhaps make a readjustment, much will be done. These are the measures that have been taken or are proposed to stimulate the housing industry and to give many thousands more Canadians access to the accommodation they require.
I might mention that we are not only interested in the production of houses but in their quality as well. I have announced a warranty system regarding the quality of a house and its continued performance over a reasonable period of time to protect home buyers. A meeting will be held early in April with representatives of provincial governments, builders, consumers, lenders, and other interested parties to consider the proposal, which is already agreed upon in principle. edl845;-l
In addition, I know that there are many innovative ideas and approaches that could provide a better quality of life within Canadian communities but that have not been tried on a large scale basis because of the cost. This is very important, because in setting up new financial measures I think my hon. friends will agree that it is important to improve the quality, to devise new and better building systems, and to devise better types of communities for Canadians to live in. It is simply not enough to put up the accommodation. It must be attractive accommodation. It must be on a human scale. It must relate to human needs.
In order to test new and different ideas in community building, CMHC is committed to a series of demonstration projects across the country. These will not be scale models, they will not be toys, but will be living communities of balanced socio-economic dimensions in which people will live and work. They should be instrumental in producing a blueprint for the future, but it will be far more than a blueprint. It will add to the housing starts in attractive ways with technology, planning, and a social approach which can be duplicated elsewhere. I am sure there will be mistakes but we will learn from those mistakes. I hope that in any program with which I am associated we will be prepared to take those chances, and be prepared to make mistakes in seeking better methods and better housing for Canadians.
The measures and proposals that I have outlined tonight have an enormous potential for housing in Canada. It is vital to their success that they be made effective efficiently and with dispatch. Recognizing this, CMHC has moved toward operational decentralization so that effective action can be taken at the local level, where the need exists. This is not an easy and simple process but is taking

place deliberately with planning and with experimentation, so that the highly qualified regional managers have a greater degree of autonomy and are tuned in better to the local situation and the local government because we are regionalized on a provincial basis now. They will be especially sensitive to the needs of the locality while bearing in mind the national objectives at all times.
I think hon. members will agree that we are meeting the housing challenge in Canada with realistic and progressive action. We cannot overlook the problems presented by world wide economic conditions, but we are determined that Canada's housing production keeps pace with our needs. We are concentrating on those programs which produce the quick starts. We have asked our provincial partners to take up these programs, and the funding that is available to them, and to accelerate this so that we get these starts and provide not only employment but the homes that are needed this year.
We know the problem is not an easy one to resolve under present economic circumstances but I assure you, Madam Speaker, we are facing up to the times and will not be found wanting.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to participate in this debate as briefly as I can because I know there is limited time and quite a number of members of the House wish to participate. I shall say very little about housing not because it is unimportant but because, quite frankly, since I have watched the way successive ministers of finance have opposed any reduction in the building tax year after year and have seen their sudden reversal when they find it politically expedient to do so, I find it difficult to take this government at all seriously in the area of housing.
May I say that it is reassuring these days to feel that the members who sit to my left who have sponsored today's motion are once again in the ranks of the opposition. I do not wish to prolong this beyond saying that I look forward to an allotted non-confidence motion by the NDP representatives in the House some day. In my time here I have seen the NDP use non-confidence motions when the government was in a majority, ostensibly to make parliament work. I have also seen them not use them during a period when they had the balance of power. In that demimonde of minority they said they did not use them on those occasions allotted to them in order to make parliament work. Without being argumentative or controversial I can only gather than the NDP logic is as much a matter of convenience as NDP principle.
This evening we are not asked to vote on the proposition put before us, so we are not obliged to take a hard and fast position on the specific request for the introduction of a new budget by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) within two weeks. I am not prepared to say that anything quite so simple as a new budget, with new spending programs, is the key to improvement of our economy, particularly an improvement which can be substained. At the same time I certainly sense the frustrations spreading around the country concerning the government's inaction. For example, I listened to the Minister of Finance this afternoon. He said they are waiting to see what will happen in respect of the United States economy. He heard a prediction from the United States Secretary of the Trea-

sury that things might turn upward in the United States in the fourth quarter.
It is impossible to find out how long the Minister of Finance will wait before he can really see the future with enough confidence to act. I doubt very much whether the Canadian people are very happy to float along in the meantime.
We have the statement that during 1974 the Canadian economy grew at a rate of 3.7 per cent. I refer to the GNP. As a matter of fact the GNP was little if any higher at the end of 1974 than at the commencement of 1974. It is merely the way in which the government brings forward statistics that suggests there was any real growth during 1974. The real growth took place in 1973, and it is the average over the year which represents a 3.7 per cent increase in 1974 over 1973. So in fact we have had virtually no growth in our economy for approximately a year.
I am sorry the Minister of Finance is not here, but he can read what I have to say in Hansard tomorrow. He spoke of how good the cash balances of the government are. Why would they not be good? Who could not sell savings bonds at a rate of 93A per cent and have the government of Canada reduce the short-term interest rate right away?
I should like the minister to admit just how much this manoeuvre will cost the Canadian taxpayers during the life of these Canada savings bonds. It will run into many billions of dollars. I think we have had enough of this kind of sleight of hand with figures, and this kind of manoeuvring which is costly to the Canadian people, while the minister boasts about having the government of Canada in a very good cash position.
The need for some action by the government surely is not a new discovery. Going back a couple of years, we had the government talking about a contingency plan to deal with an emergency situation in the economy. That contingency plan was, of course, price and income controls, as was admitted by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Nobody knows whether that particular contingency plan still exists.
Back in 1973 and early 1974 the government stalled things along by laying every increase in the cost of living at the door of shortages. For months the Minister of Finance indulged in one of the most gross over simplifications ever perpetrated in this House. For many months, with the help of my hon. friends in the NDP, he was able to get away with doing virtually nothing about high prices except to blame the weather. We are now well into 1975, and we see that the so-called consensus-and it is mainly this which I want to discuss tonight-as pursued by the government has become like the weather in at least one respect. Everyone in the government is talking about it, but no one in the government is doing anything about it.

the country that all its talk about pursuing a consensus has been just that, all talk, and part of a strategy of stalling. I say that this impression holds danger, not just for the interests of the government party, but dangers for the interests of order and confidence throughout our society.

speechtext:
Let us go back to the throne speech at the opening of this thirtieth parliament on September 30, 1974. This was the language used by the government in the Speech from the Throne, and I quote:
There must be a greater awareness of the need for restraint by everyone in what each seeks to secure in incomes, profits, prices or taxes if inflation is to be mitigated. Demands to secure more than the economy can provide, or indeed for those who already have a respectable return to seek to benefit relatively from inflation, must be resisted, and the government believes it has a clear responsibility in this area. Just as no one group in society should benefit at the expense of others from inflation, so should no one group shoulder an unfair burden.
The government has therefore initiated a series of consultations with the principal groups in our society-business, professions, farmers, labour and provincial governments.
Then a bit further on it was stated:
The federal government believes that it has the responsibility of playing the leading role in bringing Canadians together to discuss their common problems and challenges and to develop proposals for their solution.
That was the government's position going into this session almost six months ago. Note that the government said it had already initiated some discussions. No results have been reported.
Then came the budget on November 18, and here is some of the inspiring rhetoric of the Minister of Finance on that occasion, and I quote him:
We have to find a better way of reconciling the competing interests of the various groups which make up our society. No group need lose in this search. Indeed, if we succeed, all can gain because the over-all performance of the economy will be enhanced by controlling inflation.
This is why we need a national consensus about what the various groups can safely take from the economy over the next few years. Co-operation must be the watchword. We will give leadership, but we will not try to impose solutions.
Again, as in the Speech from the Throne, the promise of leadership was made.
I am glad to see that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Cullen) is here tonight.

When he tells me that he would be on a better footing to proceed with initiatives to expand the economy if he had a restraint program in place, I take that as a sensible response to a question that I put to him.
Why then, why oh why, is this minister, who expresses these concerns, and supports that premise, simply going along with the gag of this stupid game of stall? The minister may say it is not a game.
