speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in this debate on the motion sponsored by the house leader of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). He and his party are proposing, as I understand it, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), having brought two budgets before this House in a period of six months, should now bring a third.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: A real one.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
The budget of last spring was overwhelmingly endorsed by the Canadian electorate who, thanks to the party now led in this House by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, were given the opportunity to express their viewpoint in the most basic and direct method known within our democratic system.
If my recollection is correct, Madam Speaker, that particular budget and the ensuing activity resulted in the party of the hon. member losing 50 per cent of its representation in this House. The second budget has not produced the same kind of redistribution of the membership of this House only because I submit the opposition of the New Democratic Party to the November 18 budgetary measures could not at this time bring the country and the government to a standstill. Had its opposition to Bill C-49 been adequate to defeat once again the duly elected government of this country I suggest that once again the electorate would have overwhelmingly supported the government, and those responsible for voting against the budgetary measures would have suffered a second calamity at the polls. Who knows how many representatives of that same party would now be with us?
Bearing these factors in mind, Madam Speaker, can they be serious in wanting a third budget at this time, which obviously they would be duty bound to vote against? I can hardly believe that. Therefore I must conclude that there is a degree of hollowness in this motion before us. I believe it is largely a ploy on the part of the NDP to take more of the time of this House to continue debate on the budgetary measures included in Bill C-49, and this after days and
March 13, 1975

days that the opposition parties spent impeding passage of the clauses in this important bill that meant so much to the taxpayers of this country.
There is a plea before us today, Madam Speaker, for the government to introduce "within two weeks" a new budget. This proposal is coming foward at a time when the last budget has just been made law within the last two hours-when the significant measures contained in this red booklet I am holding, the budget summary, are just coming into effect. Yet it is suggested that we should immediately move to another one-that we should implement at this time a new shift in the economic policy of the country. We have hardly had an opportunity to test the effect of the most recent budget let alone had time to permit the measures to be assessed in their over-all impact on the economy in any meaningful way.
A budget is a serious document. It aims to assist in shaping economic policy over the several months to come. While economists are not in agreement on what economic ground rules should be in vogue at any one time, I believe there is general agreement that one thing that has not helped the recent economic climate within the borders of our neighbour to the south has been, on the one hand, a move to tighten significantly the economic hatches, followed shortly thereafter by a major move in the opposite direction to loosen substantially the purse strings to such an extent that Mr. Simon is quoted today as saying in Ottawa that his own country was "playing with fire".
Stability is a most important factor when the economic climate is so fragile and unpredictable. The November 18 budget provided stability with leadership, as expressed in the courses of action to be followed by this Liberal government. Surely it is hardly responsible to suggest the reopening of the whole, massive budgetary process within four months of the introduction of the last budget, and within hours of the passage of measures introduced pursuant to that budget and, yes, before, the passage of reasonable time which will permit a fair and meaningful assessment of those budgetary measures.
The shifts in government leadership and economic policy must be accorded their proper significance. Such shifts are not to be taken lightly, and we would be taking them lightly if we were to give the motion before the House serious consideration.
I wish to probe somewhat deeper the proposal of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby-assuming for the moment that he is serious in proposing that another budget should be placed before parliament and, the Canadian people soon, and I must so assume, or what we are witnessing today is an exercise in futility. He makes this proposal on the same day as royal assent is given to measures contained in the November 18 budget. On this day the New Democratic Party, for whom the hon. member speaks, requests the government to introduce another budget. The question then is, what does the hon. member and the NDP want in this new budget? What would they propose? This is a vital question since, if the new budget were introduced and did not contain measures to assuage the "dollar deficit appetite" of the New Democratic Party, that party could start the process again on the next opposi-
Canadian Economy
tion day. One can visualize this chamber being turned into a veritable budget office in which a new budget is constantly being requested just when the previously introduced budget is being considered.
It will be interesting to see how the official opposition votes on this motion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: There is no vote on it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Are they, too, anxious to turn this chamber into a forum in which little legislation can be debated, in which little is discussed except budgetary policy? I hardly think they will go along with that. Yet, Mr. Speaker, this will be their stance if their "dollar deficit appetite" induces them to support the motion moved by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby.
Is the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby really serious in wanting the Canadian national debt to be substantially augmented? Does he want the debt that we and future generations must bear to be even larger? Does the NDP not appreciate the danger of artificially over-heating the economy when inflation in the western world is at such high levels? Surely they understand that government stimulants to the economy at any time, particularly at times like the present, must be provided with a steady, firm, yet gentle hand, so that the medicine is not worse than the disease it was intended to cure. Yet that is exactly what their proposal would involve.
Not content to let current budgetary measures work their way through the economy, the NDP seeks to fuel the fires of inflation by creating artificial wealth. The government which follows such advice might purchase political popularity, but in all likelihood the serious repercussions which would follow could undermine the economic life of the country to such a degree that a normal economic stance would be difficult to achieve. At the same time it would do little or nothing to increase the production of goods when international markets are weak. And they are weak, even though Canadians would prefer them to be strong.
We are living with an international problem. Yes, there are things we can do at home, and we are doing them. However, undermining national and international confidence in our country's economy, which is surely what would happen if we were to support the proposal before us, a proposal which asks the government to change the direction of economic policy just when we have placed the stamp of approval on a major thrust which is aimed in a particular and specific direction, will not help any of us. Of course the government which I support will not conduct itself in such manner. I only hope the members of the official opposition have the good sense to follow our lead and dissociate themselves from the unreasonable and irresponsible proposal placed before the House today by the New Democratic Party.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are not asking the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to make the usual kind of budget statement. We want the government to bring in a budget which will do three specific things, and in my opinion we should bring this proposal forward on every opposition day, until the government listens.

March 13, 1975
Canadian Economy
If the government were to use for housing the $4 million which certain wrongdoers obtained through graft, the minister responsible for housing could reduce interest payments for substantial numbers of families who have bought NHA homes. Or, we could build 1,000 homes costing $40,000.
As everyone knows, the budget will bring few changes in this country, particularly to poor people. According to a recent Senate report, a great many Canadians live on or below the povery line, the poverty line for a single person in Canada now being $3,100. Old age pensioners in this country get a pension of $2,450, which is considerably below the poverty line. Statistics Canada says a family is living on or below the poverty line when it must spend 70 per cent or more of its income on basic necessities like food, shelter and clothing. In 1974, according to Statistics Canada, the poverty line for a single person was at $2,518, which is about $100 more than we paid old age pensioners.
The publication entitled "Poor Kids", which is a report by the National Council of Welfare on children in poverty in Canada, says on page 36:
There can be no hiding behind myths that we can't afford to ensure income adequacy to all Canadians. The recent federal budget proved that. The Minister of Finance redistributed $1.75 billion for the 1975-76 fiscal year through reductions in the personal income tax alone. He redistributed another $885 million of the 1975-76 national income by changes in sales tax and tariff provisions, more than half of this-$450 million-through reduction of the sales tax on building materials.
All of this $2.6 billion that the government has chosen not to collect represents a redistribution in the national income. But in what direction? The personal income tax cuts range from $200 for those in the lowest tax bracket to $750 for those in the highest. In other words, if you were too poor to pay taxes you got nothing; if you were a low-income taxpayer you got $200; but if you were already rich enough to be in the top tax bracket you got $750. The rich got most, presumably because they needed it least. Are these our values?
The deduction of $1,000 of interest and dividend income will, of course, be welcomed by all those with significant income from bank deposits and stock holdings. Self-evidently, these are not the poor.
The Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan and cut in the sales tax for building materials are designed to benefit those in the home-bying market. Again, not the poor. Even the deduction of $1,000 of pension income will benefit only the best-off of senior citizens.
Yet no one suggested we couldn't afford these tax cuts. Economists argued whether they were too much or too little economic medicine for a situation in which everything but the inflation rate was slowing down, but no one suggested we couldn't afford it.
A guaranteed adequate income that eliminates poverty in Canada will cost roughly the amount of these tax cuts-about two-and-a-half or three billion dollars. We can afford it exactly as easily as we afforded the tax cuts. The question is whether we choose to.
If a new budget were presented within two weeks it would face the problem of whether we wish to redistribute income in such a way that the poor or the rich would receive the benefit of it. Obviously the Simards, the McNamara's and others like them have done well by governments, and are doing well today. Whether or not we throw away $4 million, we can have a scandal of that magnitude, and that is probably only the tip of the iceberg.
It is my guess that when the smoke clears we will find that not only in that field but in dozens of others where the government uses the tender system, we will have squandered millions and millions of dollars. There would have been enough money for the Minister of State for

Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) to lower the interest rate,, which is the only way of enabling the average Canadian to buy a home.
Most people are not in the category where they can afford to buy food and the other necessities of life and still make payments of $300 and $400 a month to buy a house in one of our major cities. What does the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) do when he is not in the House supporting the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner)? He is making statements such as the following one:
-the question will not be whether politicians ought to believe in a more or less egalitarian society, but rather whether they are able to "read" the community's values correctly, and express them correctly in terms of basic income levels, and in terms of income distribution generally.
I again quote from the document:
What are Canadian community values? How much do we care whether for 14-year-old boy "it will always be this way"? Does it matter to us if poor kids are hungry or sick, if they are shamed out of schools and into dead-end jobs from which they are the first laid off when the economy slows down? Do the aged and disabled matter to us? Do we care as much about them as about the millionaire industrialist who benefited most from this year's income redistribution? ...
The probabilities and likelihoods which we have described in this report will remain unchanged or be transformed to an extent that will be determined by our value choice. That choice, which we the Canadian community will make, will tell us a great deal about ourselves.
We will have to make that decision. It is fine for members of this House, who make a fairly good salary, to be given tax concessions with regard to dividends and interest rates. If we have never owned a house, it is fine for us to save $1,000 a year for ten years tax free to be able to buy a very expensive house. However, would our values not be better if we put that money toward taking over one of the banking or financial institutions of this country and, instead of paying 6 Yi per cent on deposits, make that money available at 614 per cent for the social good of this nation?
Are we always going to be satisfied with living off the misery of the poor of this nation? This affects all senior citizens in this country, as well as most of our low income people. It is true that in some families two or three people are physically able to work. In that event I am sure they will be able to come up to the standard. Those three people only have to earn $6,145 to be at the poverty level. Is that our goal?
As long as there are poor in this country, if any member of parliament will say that we should not call for a new budget to end all poverty, as well as the sickness and disasters that go with being poor, he should re-examine his sense of values. Canada can only be rich when there are no poor or disadvantaged people.
I see no reason why we cannot have a budget to change our tax structure in such a way that the rich will begin to pay their share. There are four people in Canada earning $200,000 who pay no income tax at all. There are few poor people who do not pay income tax. If we settle for anything less we will not be doing the best we can for the Canadian people and the future of this nation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few comments on the NDP motion for a new budget, as well as on the mounting unemployment

and housing problem. I am well aware that money does not grow on trees. I believe the budget for this year with the supplementary estimates will be in the neighbourhood of $26.53 billion. That is an awful lot of money Canadians will have to raise for various government projects. I am also aware that we have a high rate of unemployment, 6.8 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Very high.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
It is very high. I am sure members on all sides of the House want to do everything possible to reduce it. There are government work programs and we all hope they will work. This brings to mind the Capital winter works program of a couple of years ago. I believe it involved a total of $150 million which money was distributed among municipalities across Canada. It resulted in the building of many worthwhile projects. Municipalities were loaned money at good rates, between 7 and 8 per cent. They received a forgiveness of 100 per cent of the labour costs if the work was done in the winter period, and 50 per cent during periods when there was not high unemployment. I hope the minister and the government will consider reintroducing that program.
If the money is not available, maybe it could be taken from some other place. I wonder about some government departments where the priority is not so high. I have the greatest sympathy for the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson). His target is $1.4 billion. I think he should have considerably more than that. Some government projects could very well be pared without causing any great crisis. I think of the CBC, which some people call the "crazy broadcasting corporation", which has a budget of $225 million. Certain programs aired by that august body would have been better left in the can. By that I mean the can for the film.
I am also told that the CBC news offices in Toronto or whatever you call them, have a tremendous number of staff there just to get together and administer the 11 o'clock news program. I believe it is one of the largest newsrooms on the whole of the North American Continent, and that certainly covers plenty of territory. Money could surely be saved on this operation. I am sure there are a great many expenditures which could be classed as frills. The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) certainly has within his jurisdiction a number of high-sounding wonderful programs, but I do not think they can be regarded as bread and butter issues.
There is another direction in which money could be saved. I have in mind these palaces, these huge civil service castles in which the mandarins live. I think that as long as the poor civil servants are kept dry in reasonably good offices, no great harm is being done. Members of parliament manage to get along in offices which are many years old, but it seems that the delicate civil servants need air conditioning, palatial offices and so on. I believe money could be saved here.
I understand the federal budget includes provision for consulting fees totalling $900 million. That is a hell of a lot of consulting fees. The Company of Young Canadians has a budget of $4.9 million. Well, there may be some good
Canadian Economy
projects under way here, but again this is not a top priority. Then there is a firm about which we have heard a lot recently, Marine Industries Limited. I believe that $250 million has been allocated to this company through the Export Development Corporation by way of a loan at very favourable interest rates between 7 and 8 per cent. Then again, we have also lent Iran, not a poverty-stricken nation, $1.5 million at an interest rate of 7 per cent.
I appreciate what the minister is doing though, naturally, he will be able to do more; we hope he can find more money to get housing production on the rails and build more units as soon as possible. The minister maintains that a sizeable amount of private money is likely to be poured into housing. I am aware-it was mentioned earlier by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters)-that the present budget allows for $1,000 to be tax free, provided it is earned by way of bank interest or bond interest. I believe that in 1975 the concession will include dividends. I certainly feel that rather than see this money staying in the banks, the Minister of Urban Affairs should be able to encourage the use of these funds as private mortgage money.
If a private individual wishes to put out his money by way of a mortgage, why should he not be given the same concession? It might surprise the minister how much money would flow into mortgages if this were allowed, and how much additional housing could be provided. I do not think this is a crazy idea. I think it has merit, and perhaps the Minister of Urban Affairs could suggest it to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner).
I am well aware there are certain types of housing which the federal government is sponsoring 100 per cent. These concern federally oriented programs, AHOP and the rest. I hope the government will reconsider its attitude and change AHOP-that it will return to the situation which existed before July and allow the scheme to apply to existing homes in rural areas. Maybe I am slightly biased, but there are a great many people who cannot afford to buy or build a new home. If they were able to buy an existing older home, qualify under AHOP and fix it up later, the former owner might well move into a new home, and housing would be generated in the long run.
Again, I hope the government will see fit to divert more money into low rental housing for senior citizens rather than extend the federally oriented programs to which I have referred. The provinces and the municipalities have a very good idea of the type of housing which is needed and where it should be built. They are already contributing to the cost of construction on this basis, though not to the same extent, proportionately, as the federal government. Consideration should be given, in my view, to providing a cheaper type of housing than that which is currently available.
Another aspect with which I should like to deal relates to rural and native housing-I mentioned this in the housing committee. Naturally, those of us who live in the rural areas when we look at the concrete jungles of Montreal, Vancouver, and, yes, even of Ottawa, and see new buildings going up all the time, wonder why some of that money cannot go into the smaller towns and villages. I am hoping something can be done to this end.

March 13, 1975
Canadian Economy
Again, on the subject of native and rural housing, I draw attention to the fact that the cost of land in rural areas is much lower than it is in the cities, and that consequently dollars spent on housing will go a lot further, bearing in mind that it costs a minimum of $20,000 for a lot in Toronto, Vancouver, or possibly in Ottawa at the present time.
Another thing the provinces have requested in the housing field: is that they be given prior notice of the housing projects the minister is dreaming up, instead of having to read about them in that Liberal clarion paper, the Globe and Mail. The provinces would like to know about these things in advance. There is something else the provincial governments want. They would like commitments from the federal government over, say, three years in advance so that they could plan ahead with assurance, and not be obliged to go cap in hand to Ottawa. I trust the minister will do what he said he would do in committee and give the provinces a three-year forecast.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am pleased to speak on this opposition day. In particular I should like to direct my words to the motion of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) on how the government is coping, and I quote from the words of the hon. member, with "the scourge of poverty". My own experience has dealt with one federal policy which is put forward for people with lower incomes, and that comes from legal aid experience. Tonight I should like to direct my words in my capacity as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
I should like to take all the members here tonight back to April, 1973, when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) tabled the working paper on social security in Canada. Our government has always maintained that the best security for the individual is a good job. There is no need to go into this at this time, but the many programs developed by the Department of Manpower and Immigration such as LIP, LEAP, OFY, as well as other working programs under DREE, all show the concern of the government for keeping the individual in the work force.
In the working paper there were five principal strategies. These were an employment strategy, a social insurance strategy, an incomes supplementation strategy, a social services strategy and a federal-provincial strategy. Substantial progress has been made since April, 1973, toward the realization of these strategies.
On the first strategy federal-provincial ministers have agreed that a community employment strategy is needed. To this end 20 developmental projects have been launched across Canada by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) and provincial ministers. This developmental work can only increase the experience of the government in finding and developing employment for people.

The object of the social insurance strategy was to enable all Canadians to make provision for their retirement through social insurance plans and to insure themselves against temporary losses of income due to sickness, accident, unemployment or maternity. The Canada and Quebec pension plans have been amended so as to increase maximum monthly retirement pensions, from $90 in December, 1973, to something like $250 in January, 1980. These changes were made in the context of the increase in old age security pensions in 1972 from $80 to $100, and the full indexation of both pensions as announced in 1973. Taken together these measures mean that total maximum old age pensions in 1975 amount to about $241 a month for a single person and $361 for a couple both over 65 in receipt of one Canada pension.
The object of the income supplementation strategy was to ensure adequate incomes for people who are working but whose incomes are not sufficient to meet family needs, and equally for people who are retired or unable to work or find employment. This objective is being accomplished for people 65 years of age and over by the increases in OAS as well as in the Canada pension plan and Quebec pension plan pensions, as I have already mentioned. Since October, 1973, the old age security pension for a single person has been increased from $100 to approximately $123.42 this April. This is probably one of the largest increases ever made over such a short period of time.
Another part of the government's income supplementation strategy is the guaranteed annual income supplement. With the cost of living indexation, as of April 1, 1975, a single person could receive a maximum old age security pension and guaranteed income supplement of $209.99 a month and a couple would receive $400.60.
As for the social services strategy, this was designed to ensure that over a period of time social services would be available to enable people to achieve their full potential. Services such as rehabilitation, vocational training, day care and home maker assistance are often required to enable people to enter or to retain useful employment, or sometimes simply to assist them to realize fuller potential as citizens.
One major national measure that was of help to a lot of working adults with families was the introduction of day care centres in 1974. The spouses of these families were able to use day care centres on the basis of need.
The fifth strategy, the federal-provincial strategy, was designed to ensure the harmonization of federal and provincial social security systems, while providing to the provinces the flexibility they required in order to adapt such systems to the needs of their citizens. For example, under the new Family Allowances Act provinces can vary the federal family allowance payment according to age or the number of children in the family. These variations were subject to a national minimum and a national average per child paid in each province.
The social policy review has progressed to the stage where it was agreed at the February, 1975, meeting of federal and provincial ministers of welfare that a policy framework for the next stages in the reform of Canada's social security system be set up. This framework would
March 13, 1975

work toward the provision of an income support program for individuals not able to enter the labour force because they were handicapped, or because there was no job available in the area, or because a single parent had family responsibilities. In addition there should be supplementation of earnings, with the creation of a work incentive measure to ensure that every Canadian would be better off at work than receiving income support.
Before concluding this review of the progress made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the government over the last two years at federal-provincial meetings, one must remember the economic climate in which this progress is being made. Our economy has been growing at a rapid rate over the last four or five years and the government has been allocating a large part of that growth toward alleviating the burdens and sometimes the distress of the lower income members of the Canadian community.
The federal government will continue to be concerned for the well being of the community as a whole. I should like to quote a statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare at the February provincial health ministers meeting. At page 14 of his speech he said:
So long as it lies within the power of the government of Canada, it will not be the poor and the economically weak who will be asked to bear the brunt of economic difficulties confronted by the western world.
May I sum up by saying that as a result of these meetings and the framework that now lies between the federal and provincial ministers of welfare, the Minister of National Health and Welfare views this framework from two perspectives. It will be designed to provide an income to those who have been unable to find jobs and to reinforce the work incentives for all who are working but at low wages. This can only help the economy over a long period and will also provide some kind of assurance that the legitimate needs of all Canadians in need of assistance will be met.
This illustrates that the government is aware of the needs of all individuals in Canada. It has shown its concern by providing innovative and new programs of the kind I have already referred to in my speech tonight. These programs have already been referred to by other speakers on behalf of the government, such as the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) who discussed the housing needs of all Canadians. As I have said, this illustrates the government is concerned about the economy of this country. I see my time has expired, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of the official opposition representing an area of Canada that has shared the problems caused for all Canadians by the government's mishandling of the economy, I am pleased to take part in this debate tonight. To restore the health of our economy will take more than a new budget. I fear it will take new leadership in Canada.
Since coming to Ottawa I have become aware that, for the members of this administration, power is not a means to an end, a tool for doing away with the injustices in our society and for alleviating the problems of many Canadians. Instead, the holding of power has become an end in
Canadian Economy
itself. Canadians have become cynical about those of us in politics, and they have every reason to be cynical. They question whether the government has any goals for our society, any blueprint for the future, and they fear that it prefers the trappings of office to the potential that possession of public office holds for making this a freer and more humane society.
Even the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his supporters must feel a twinge of embarrassment to recall the promises made in the summer of 1968 that a new administration under this Prime Minister would provide Canadians with a just society, because during his six and a half years as Prime Minister the inequities among our citizens have increased instead of declined, the freedom of individual Canadians to live their lives in peace has been further restricted by ever-increasing taxes and miles of new government red tape, and our economy has been laid waste by a government without the will or the imagination to bring in strong measures to put our economic affairs in order.
In my own constituency, which is located in the heart of our most prosperous province, the effects of the government's failure to provide leadership have been deeply felt. Our people are among the most industrious and most fiercely independent anywhere in this country, but our small businessmen are smothered by bureaucratic restrictions and taxed almost to the point where they would be better to close their doors.
Our farmers, many of whom have been on the same land for several generations, are leaving their farms in record numbers. Our working men are being laid off as the effects of the current recession deepen. Our senior citizens have found their life savings stolen by the tax of inflation, and many of them do not even know where they will find the money for next month's rent. Our young people are beginning to realize that their hopes of some day owning a home of their own have vanished. The memory of last summer's election campaign when they were told by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) that "leadership is the issue" is a bitter memory in the winter of 1975.
If our farmers are to stay on the land they need more than hollow promises from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), because promises will not cover their production costs. If small business men are to continue in business they need more than smug assurances that the problems are worse in France, or Germany, or the Soviet Union. If the working people are to save for their retirement they need to know that their savings will not be taxed away either directly to finance governmental empire building or indirectly through the menace of inflation.
I am appalled that it is necessary to remind the Minister of Finance that there is more to being a minister of the Crown than driving around in a chauffeured limousine, or attending important meetings in other countries, or having battalions of assistants to make work for each other. He has a responsibility second only to that of the Prime Minister to provide leadership in solving this country's problems.

March 13, 1975
Canadian Economy
A couple of years ago the Prime Minister said that any government which could not come to grips with self-inflicted inflation deserved to be thrown from office. The Prime Minister needs to be reminded of that statement because, as long as it is in office only this government can introduce new policies that will resolve our economic problems. If it continues to refuse to act it should be removed from office.
The Minister of Finance has been decisive in rejecting the proposals we have made for our economy. He has rejected our proposals for a price and income policy, and he has had the government members stand up twice to defeat our proposal to return some $500 million to the taxpayers. Surely his responsibility goes beyond rejecting other peoples proposals. Surely he has a responsibility to come back to the people of Canada with some proposals of his own.
What is the economic policy of the government? For one thing, it has decided to bring in a record budget with an increase in terms of main estimates of 28.2 per cent. This big spending Minister of Finance has made his predecessor look penurious by comparison.
Look at what has happened to federal expenditures under this government. In 1968 when the Prime Minister took office every man, woman and child in Canada paid an average tax of about $550. Today the figure is about $1,325. In 1968 the federal budget was $12 billion. It had taken this country over 100 years to reach that figure, but today, six years later, the budget is about two and a half times that size, and the total proportion of our gross national product now controlled by government at one level or another is about 40 per cent.
The Minister of Finance is travelling around the country discussing the need for restraint in business and labour. The details of the proposal he is making are secret. While the details are being kept secret from the Canadian public it is clear that he is asking them to exercise some restraint for the common good.
If we cannot give the Minister of Finance any credit for demonstrating courage in dealing with the economy, we can at least acknowledge that he has demonstrated he has a lot of nerve when it comes to asking private businesses and individual men and women to show self-restraint for the public good at the very same time he and his colleagues wallow in the excesses of waste and extravagance being paid for by the taxpayers' earnings.
What I would like to do today is provide the House with a few examples of the exploding amount of waste financed by money coerced by this government from the taxpayers. One of the areas in which this waste is most apparent is in the federal government's information bureaucracy. An excellent series of articles was prepared recently by the Canadian Press, and they give some interesting facts about the waste in this section of government.
In the past five years the information bureaucracy has doubled in size, and now includes 863 people at a cost of $200 million a year. There are also some 403 vacancies. Of course most of the propaganda work is contracted out, generally to Liberal advertising agencies that dream up campaigns to try to convince you that the post office feels "Your Mail is Vital", or that the problems of women in

Canada can be solved by wearing a "Why Not" button, or that filling out your tax form this year is really easier than you think.
Perhaps it is because the government has become so conscious of its image that it refused to release a 1973 survey which deals with this matter. Many members of this House will recall the reports recently about the minister of health's speech to this chamber in which he defended his decision to deny Canadians the right to watch WFL games. Those remarks, which none of us had realized were worth much at all at the time, cost the taxpayers a total of $1,950, about 36 cents a word.
Many of us do not realize that the minister has also done well in the government's television sweepstakes, creating within his department a television studio that, according to one information officer, anybody would be proud to own. His officials showed their resourcefulness in 1972 when they dispatched a film crew to the 1972 Munich Olympics. When they were denied permission to film the games because they had not bothered to get proper credentials, they took pictures of the stadium which became part of a 25 minute children's film entitled "It's not the winning". Apparently it was not.
According to Canadian Press, the minister's department developed an $80,000 television studio in Tunney's Pasture where it had ambitious plans to produce television shows. Since then the plans have fallen through and the equipment is now used for such purposes as filming autopsies on farm animals.
Last fall one of my constituents wrote asking me to look into the research and development contracts being handed out by the Department of Supply and Services. We have spent a considerable amount of time reviewing the activities of that branch of the government over the past couple of years. As members will know, in August of 1972 the government announced a new policy designed to encourage research and development to be done for the government by the private sector. The government was concerned about the scientific bureaucracy within government, and it decided it should try to spread the wealth, sharing it with the private sector.
A new bulletin will be released soon by Supply and Services, but their last one which includes the contracts awarded up until January 31 shows that some $26,960,986 had been given out between last April 1 and the end of this January. That figure represents a considerable increase over the same period last year.
None of us on this side of the House would dispute the value of the government showing leadership in the field of research and development. Nor would we quarrel with the policy of having much more of this work done by the private sector. We do most certainly look with skepticism at a number of the projects and the way they have been handled. Some seem to be extremely wasteful, but may indeed be justifiable. If they are, I would welcome the government's explanation. I would also welcome explanations in respect of projects which cannot easily be justified.
Let us take a look at some of these contracts. In October of 1974 the government reported a contract of $3,000 for "preparation of six newspaper articles describing the work

of the environmental protection service". The payment of $500 an article would be enough to make any reporter in the press gallery begin to salivate. What is also interesting about this contract is that it went to a chap in Victoria who, up until last summer, was employed as an information officer with the public information branch of the environmental protection service. It is too bad that they could not have got him to do the work while he was on salary.
Also in the October bulletin was the report of a contract for $40,500 to "Canadian Facts" of Toronto for "a survey of Canadian public awareness of scientific developments and achievements as obtained through the news media". No doubt that is a worthy project if you have $40,000 sitting around.
In the same bulletin it was reported that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce had a contract for "a study, through selected methods of human reactions to the introduction of the metric system in Quebec". This little gem will cost a mere $65,000.
In the same issue it is reported that a decision was made that a fellow from Bergen, Norway, should also get a piece of the action. He will be receiving $1,250 for the "preparation of a lecture on Norwegian developments in ultra-sonic methods of current measurements".
In July of 1974 a contract for $9,560 went for an "analytical study of methods to popularise science and technology". That sounds like a great way to spend an extra $9,560.
I see that I am quickly approaching the end of my time. There are many other examples I could give of extravagant waste within the government. For example, a sizable grant was given in respect of the "interpretation of data available on the site-change responses of native trees in the national capital region."
I would invite hon. members of this House to avail themselves of these editions of the Department of Supply and Service bulletins, in order to see the sort of grants being given out by that department. A new bulletin will become available in the next couple of days. It disturbs me that at the same time the Minister of Finance is asking Canadians to show restraint he continues to indulge in this type of waste and extravagance. As I said at the beginning, perhaps it will take a new budget to put our economic house in order. But even more than that, the fact is that we need new leadership in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by thanking the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who agreed I might have five minutes of his short time to put forward a few remarks.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
I would be grateful if my colleagues would applaud the hon. member rather than me.
In a very summary way I might observe that no one in this debate on this side of the House has by any means indicated we are proud of the unemployment rate in this country, the rate of inflation or the rate of growth. I do not say that. But by international standards of performance
Canadian Economy
we are doing better than the major powers around the world, some of which are going bankrupt.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Name one.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Italy, to name one. I think it is a tribute to the minister that he has been listened to specifically for leadership by the most powerful nations in order to try to find solutions to these international problems. I noted in the remarks of the minister that he did not foreclose the possibility of a new budget being introduced some time soon. I am sure he would introduce one if it were considered to be helpful. In this spirit I should like to make some suggestions in respect of areas where activities might take place, if international activity evaporates, and where internal activity might be generated to provide real growth and real jobs. First, we in Canada have something few other countries have; we have our frontier. When our foreign markets decline we can turn to this frontier and direct our energies and full productive capacities to developing it.
There must be ten projects on the shelf which are of tremendous magnitude, any one of which would be a great stimulus to the economy. One has been committed. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) should be congratulated for Syncrude. The very decision to proceed with Syncrude has tremendous impact on our economy, not only in the west where the centre of gravity will be but in all parts of the country. And there are other projects on the shelf, such as pipelines for oil and gas, electrical plants in Fundy and James Bay, and offshore development and exploration projects. I think it may be time for the government to look on the shelf and indicate that some of these projects should be proceeded with, giving heed to the ecology and to human-considerations. The green light should be turned on. However, the frontier is only one place to go.
There is another industry whose entire production is domestically consumed and for which world markets are not needed. That is the housing industry. It is the classic generator of economic action including production of roads, schools, parks, furniture, carpets, appliances, and 100 other things which go when housing goes. It is the best generator of jobs at all levels of skills. It is a decentralized industry which can provide action in every community in Canada.
Apart from all the economic considerations, housing is badly needed. In my own riding rents may go up 25 per cent in the next year. In this spirit I would urge the government to take action. The federal government can give housing a big push. It has done so in the past. Last year of over $1,200,000,000 offered to this country in housing, less than $1 billion, only about $900 million, was taken up. The government can give such encouragement and should continue to do so.
Government stimulated production has always followed tax reductions. I wish to make the suggestion that the next budget, instead of stimulating by tax reductions, should stimulate by special new housing programs. CMHC has the ideas. The minister knows what he wants to do. What is needed are more funds for land acquisition, for servicing, for sewers, for roads, for mortgages and for subsidiz-

March 13, 1975
Canadian Economy
ing interest rates and rents for public housing. Let us call the next budget a housing budget.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO IMPROVE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the key words in the motion we have been debating today are the last four words, "the scourge of poverty". Some hon. members across the way do not like those words appearing in this sedate House of Commons, but I suggest it is one of the facts of life in Canada today to which we really must address ourselves with all the seriousness at our command.
Members who know anything of the conditions in the outports of Newfoundland, in the core areas of our cities or among the native peoples, and those who are aware of the fact that about a million of our senior citizens receive the guaranteed income supplement because they have nothing else, will have to agree that there is in this affluent land of ours a scourge of poverty that could be very serious for us in the years that lie ahead.
I congratulate the National Council of Welfare on the several reports it has produced in recent years, particularly its report entitled "Prices and the Poor," which appeared in April, 1974, and also its report entitled "Poor Kids" which was published in March 1975, just a week or two ago. This latter report has been referred to frequently today and is one which I believe every member of this House should read.
The fact is that although we may be afraid of what will happen to us in Canada or in the world because of pollution, the lack of energy, nuclear war or what have you, I submit that when in Canada there are over 1,600,000 children living in poverty, our future is not very bright.
Among the various documents which have come to our attention in recent months which underline the scourge of poverty is a copy of a speech made in Toronto on October 31, 1974, by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) entitled "Income Distribution: A question of community ethics". It was a tremendous speech in which, although he referred to the gains we have made in social welfare, the minister pointed out that despite all those gains the distribution of wealth in this country is still terribly unequal, with a very large number of Canadian individuals and families living below the poverty line. This is a challenge this country must meet, and I trust members on all sides will pay no attention to those who say that our asking for a new budget is just a ploy, but will listen to the sort of things that were said earlier by my colleague the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), and will realize that the future of this country really depends on our solving this problem, getting rid of poverty and inequality and making sure that the wealth we produce is distributed as equally as possible among all our people. This has to be our goal.

subtopic: PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE-INCREASE IN EXPENDITURES REFLECTED IN ESTIMATES
PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE-INCREASE IN EXPENDITURES REFLECTED IN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the recently tabled main estimates Blue Book there are many shocking and amazing figures, but none more shocking or amazing than the 29 per cent jump in the budget for the Prime Minister's office, with corresponding increase for the Privy Council office and cabinet secretariat.
In the 1974-75 fiscal year the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) somehow got by with a staff of only 95 and a mere $1,643,000 budget. But for 1975-76 he has apparently decided that he cannot operate on that meagre stipend, so the
March 13, 1975

budget is for $2,124,000 and a staff of 101-over $2 million to operate the Prime Minister's office and residence.
In 1962-63 the total budget for the Prime Minister's residence was $23,930. This was broken down under six headings. The Prime Minister's office was funded by the Privy Council office which had a total administration budget of $563,600. This year the Privy Council has an operational budget of over $14.5 million, without counting capital expenditure or grants. This is a direct increase of $3,241,000 over last year, or a 28.7 per cent jump for the second year in a row.
Few of these figures are broken down substantially. They are left in blocks of $2 million, $3 million or even $6 million under nebulous titles and descriptions. In the estimates in the early 1960's expenditures were explicitly described down to amounts in the hundreds of dollars, so that we knew how the Prime Minister was spending taxpayers' money.
Now the estimates allot $2.1 million under the heading of the office of the Prime Minister, with no further explanation than the operation of the office of the Prime Minister, maintenance of his residence and allowances to former prime ministers, the latter of which is only $5,556. These figures raise some very serious doubts. Where is all this money going, what is it used for, and why is it necessary? If the Prime Minister feels he can justify these expenditures, he should voluntarily table a full breakdown. If he does not think he can justify them, it is imperative that the House insist on receiving this explanation so that the Canadian people can see how their money is being squandered.
It is becoming tragically apparent that this incredible amount of money is being used by the Prime Minister to surround himself with an army of politically appointed personal advisers who are facilitating the concentration of power in the Prime Minister, usurping the role of parliament, and duplicating the work of the senior public service and even the cabinet.
The Prime Minister is apparently conducting an experiment in running the country from his office, and as a result we are heading toward the U.S. presidential system of government in this country. Parliament has been emasculated, and the morale of the senior levels of the civil service has never been lower. This experiment of giving presidential power to the Prime Minister has obviously been a dismal failure. The evidence is all around us. Hon. members simply have to pick up a newspaper, or glance through their daily mail when it is delivered, to see proof that civil unrest and public dissatisfaction are at an all time high.
In 1974 our country lost 9.5 million working days because of strikes-67 per cent more than in 1973, and more than any other industrialized nation except one. We all know what is happening now in 1975.
And, of course, the main reason for the unprecedented magnitude of strikes is the unpredecented magnitude of inflation that has been cultivated by the government. Apparently the group of seven did not have any more
Adjournment Debate
effective solutions than the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), nor does either have any ideas to ease our unemployment rate, which is at 6.8 per cent and rising.
It is abundantly clear that the result of the Prime Minister's experiment are not positive. In fact the experiment is very damaging to the country as a whole during the present trying economic period, and will be permanently damaging to the institution of parliament, the make-up of the civil service and the very system of government in our country.
The Prime Minister must take immediate steps to return the power of governing to parliament before that power is irreparably eroded. He must cease surrounding himself with a huge staff of personal appointees who are loyal only to him and not to the government as a whole, as is the permanent civil service with which his advisers are in competition. He must begin to show some example of frugality and restraint to a country that is desperately in need of some form of leadership from the government in the fight against inflation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leonard Hopkins (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE-INCREASE IN EXPENDITURES REFLECTED IN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I must say that the remarks of the hon. gentleman have been addressed to the House as a member of the opposition and that in many ways they can be refuted because he has quoted figures that go back to the early 1960's. But today we are living in 1975 and I am sure the Canadian people will realize that not only have costs risen since the early 1960's but also that the Canadian people have written to their members of parliament, and certainly to members of cabinet, and to the Prime Minister's office, in far greater extent in this modern age than they did in the early 1960's. I think it is only fair to say they expect answers to those requests.
Mr. Speaker, it should be pointed out that the operation of the Prime Minister's office is included within the estimates of the Privy Council office. As far as the estimates for the Prime Minister's Office are concerned, the cost of its operation has been carefully scrutinized by the Privy Council and the Treasury Board and it is entirely within the practices and procedures of the government. The increased estimates do reflect the side effects of inflation which is the case with all levels of government and within the private sector.
In the case of the over-all estimates for the Privy Council office it should be remembered that additional funds are required to support an expanded responsibility in the field of federal-provincial relations which are necessary in a federal society, and which was recognized in a bill passed by this House last December.
In conclusion, I can only say that I think it is more important than ever before today that Canadians have a personal liaison with members of cabinet, with members of parliament, and with the Prime Minister's office in particular than they have ever had. That process is going on, and I think this is a very valid argument in this particular case.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.12 p.m.
